[CH01 | 00:00-00:42 | promise_setup]

So you want to own a lottery store.

Makes sense. It's the only business where probability guarantees profit on every ticket sold — and half the people who open one still go broke within three years.

Here's the problem: selling lottery tickets is mathematically bulletproof revenue. The state pays you a commission on everything that moves through your register. Every scratch-off, every Powerball, every draw game.

And yet lottery retailers close constantly.

So what breaks?

---

[CH02 | 00:42-01:34 | context_expansion]

Let's start with what it costs to get in.

Three tiers.

Bottom tier: you rent a corner inside an existing convenience store. Lottery machine, display rack, maybe eight square feet. You're looking at $5,000 to $15,000 in equipment and your first inventory buy. Think gas stations, delis, small grocers.

Middle tier: standalone storefront. Dedicated lottery retailer. Now you're signing a lease, installing security, building out shelving, stocking a full wall of instant tickets. $50,000 to $120,000 all-in. Real examples: New York, New Jersey, California — dedicated lottery shops exist in strip malls next to nail salons.

Top tier: franchise or multi-location operation. You're not just selling tickets, you're building a regional brand. Initial investment starts at $250,000, can run past half a million depending on location count and build-out. Think chains like Lottery USA — real players operating multiple locations with shared back-office systems.

The gap between tiers isn't just money. It's scale, margin compression, and infrastructure weight.

---

[CH03 | 01:34-02:49 | evidence_build]

But the real entry ticket isn't cash.

It's permission.

Most states cap the total number of lottery licenses. Massachusetts, for instance — 7,500 active retailers statewide, zero new licenses issued in some counties for years. Want in? You buy out someone who already has one, or you wait until someone closes.

Then there's geography. California requires population density thresholds — you can't open within a certain radius of an existing retailer unless the area supports it. Some states mandate minimum distance between locations: 1,000 feet, half a mile, depends on the market.

And then the approval process itself. Background checks, credit reviews, site inspections. Timeline? Anywhere from 90 days to over a year. One applicant in Florida waited 14 months for final approval — by the time the license arrived, the lease had expired.

In tight markets, licenses trade like assets. A New York City bodega license with lottery rights can sell for $30,000 above the business value, just for the privilege of selling tickets.

The scarcity isn't accidental. It's engineered.

---

[CH04 | 02:49-04:52 | reveal]

Now the money.

Imagine you sell $100 worth of lottery tickets in a single transaction. Depending on the state and the game type, you keep between $5 and $7 of that.

That's your commission. Instant tickets — scratch-offs — typically pay 5% to 6%. Draw games like Powerball or Mega Millions pay a bit more, around 6% to 7%, because the state wants to incentivize promotion of big jackpot games.

So if your store moves $10,000 in lottery sales in a week, you're taking home $500 to $700 in commission.

Scale that up. A mid-volume standalone location doing $500,000 in annual lottery sales pulls roughly $30,000 in commission. A high-traffic convenience store pushing $2 million a year? $120,000 to $140,000.

But here's the split that matters: instant tickets vs draw games.

Instant tickets are impulse buys. Customer walks in, sees the wall, grabs three $5 scratch-offs on the way out. High frequency, low friction. Draw games require a slip, a selection, often a wait. Lower frequency, but bigger ticket averages when jackpots climb.

In practice, instant tickets account for 60% to 70% of total sales at most retailers. They're the engine. Draw games are the headline, but scratch-offs are the daily grind that keeps the register moving.

The state takes its cut first — roughly 60% to 65% goes to the prize pool, another 25% to 30% funds state programs. What's left after prizes and state allocation is split between administrative overhead and retailer commission.

Your slice is thin. But it's guaranteed.

---

[CH05 | 04:52-05:45 | reveal]

Here's the category nobody talks about: $1 and $2 instant tickets.

Lowest price point. Highest volume. Fastest repeat purchase cycle.

Commission rate on these? Often better than expensive tickets. Why? Because the state wants movement. A $1 ticket at 6% commission moves ten times faster than a $20 ticket at 5%. The math favors velocity.

And the customer? The one buying $2 scratch-offs every other day isn't the guy dropping $50 on a single $20 ticket. It's the regular. The construction worker stopping in every morning. The retiree buying two tickets with coffee.

That person — unremarkable, predictable, forgettable — is statistically your most valuable customer.

The $20 ticket buyer shows up when the jackpot hits $500 million. The $2 ticket buyer shows up 200 times a year.

Frequency beats ticket size. Always.

---

[CH06 | 05:45-06:31 | evidence_build]

So how do you engineer frequency?

Space.

The scratch-off wall goes behind the counter, eye level, fully stocked. Not off to the side. Not in a drawer. Front and center, within arm's reach of the transaction.

The register? Positioned so the customer has to stand there, facing the wall, while you ring them up. Thirty seconds of exposure. Enough time to scan, spot a new game, impulse-buy.

Successful retailers rotate stock weekly. New games get prime placement. Sold-out games disappear immediately — empty slots kill momentum.

And the checkout counter itself: narrow the path, slow the exit. Not enough to frustrate, just enough to create a pause. That pause is where the add-on happens.

The goal isn't to sell once. It's to train the weekly return.

---

[CH07 | 06:31-07:18 | evidence_build]

Then there's loyalty.

Some states allow second-chance drawings. Customer loses on a scratch-off, enters the ticket code online, gets another shot at a prize. It costs the retailer nothing, but it keeps the player engaged with your location as the entry point.

Others permit in-store promotions: "Buy five tickets, get one free." Technically, the retailer eats the cost of that sixth ticket, but the math works if it converts a monthly buyer into a weekly buyer.

Look at lifetime value. An occasional customer spends maybe $200 a year. A regular? $1,500 to $2,000. The free ticket is a $5 investment to capture a $1,300 gap.

Casinos figured this out decades ago: give away the cheap thing to lock in the expensive behavior.

Lottery retailers are learning.

---

[CH08 | 07:18-08:35 | reveal]

Now the top of the pyramid.

The top 5% of lottery customers — high-frequency players spending $100 to $200 a week — can account for 30% to 40% of a store's total commission revenue.

One case: a retailer in Pennsylvania reported a single customer who spent $15,000 annually on scratch-offs. At 6% commission, that's $900 from one person. Multiply by five or ten regulars at that tier, and you've just covered rent.

But they don't only buy lottery tickets.

They buy cigarettes. Energy drinks. Snacks. Lottery traffic is foot traffic, and foot traffic converts.

Gross margin on tobacco: 8% to 12%. On beverages: 20% to 35%. On packaged snacks: 25% to 40%. A high-volume lottery store in a good location can pull an additional $40,000 to $80,000 annually from ancillary sales driven by lottery customers.

The formula is:

**Commission rate × sales volume × purchase frequency × ancillary conversion**

Optimize any one variable, revenue climbs. Optimize all four, you're running a real business.

This is how a lottery store works when it works.

---

[CH09 | 08:35-10:46 | conflict_escalation]

Now the part that kills people.

Rent. For a standalone storefront in a decent location, you're paying $2,500 to $6,000 a month. High-traffic urban zones? Double that.

Labor. You can't leave a lottery terminal unattended. Minimum one employee per shift, often two. At $15/hour, that's $30,000 to $50,000 annually for basic coverage.

The lottery terminal itself: leased from the state lottery commission, usually $50 to $150 per month depending on the state. Non-negotiable.

Inventory. Instant tickets require upfront cash. You order $10,000 in scratch-offs, you pay $10,000. If they don't sell, you're holding dead inventory. The state eventually takes them back, but you've tied up cash for weeks or months.

Then there's the state's cut on your total revenue — not just prizes. Some states charge a licensing fee, an annual renewal, or a percentage override on gross sales. It's small, 1% to 2%, but it's another line item.

And cash handling. Lottery retailers move a lot of cash. Armored car pickup, safe rental, theft insurance, cash variance — it adds up. Estimate $500 to $1,500 a month depending on volume.

Oh, and unredeemed ticket liability. If you sell a winning ticket and the customer never claims it, the state keeps the prize, but you still owe them the funds for the ticket sold. It's rare, but it's a hidden float cost.

Add it up. Let's say you're pulling $40,000 in annual lottery commission. Rent takes $36,000. Labor takes $40,000. You're already underwater before utilities, insurance, inventory float, and terminal lease.

The commission is guaranteed. Everything else is a knife fight.

---

[CH10 | 10:46-12:55 | conflict_escalation]

Real failure looks like this.

Case one: 2018, New Jersey. Investor opens a standalone lottery shop in a suburban strip mall. Total buildout: $90,000. Projected annual sales: $1.2 million based on nearby demographics.

Actual sales: $320,000. Turns out the demographics were right, but the foot traffic was wrong. The anchor tenant — a grocery store — had closed six months earlier. No anchor, no traffic. Store lasted 11 months, closed owing $30,000 in back rent, sold fixtures for $8,000.

Lesson: foot traffic isn't a demographic projection. It's a physical headcount you verify in person.

Case two: 2020, Florida. Experienced retailer opens a second location with $50,000 in startup capital. Rent is $4,000/month, labor is $3,500/month, fixed costs run $8,000 monthly before inventory.

Sales start slower than expected. He dips into working capital to cover month two. Then month three. By month five, he's tapped out. Lottery sales were fine — $25,000 in commission over five months — but it wasn't enough to cover the burn rate. Closed after six months, lost the entire $50,000.

Lesson: don't open on a cash cushion that assumes perfection from day one.

Both cases share the same pattern: the revenue model worked. The math was sound. Location or cash flow broke them.

The commission delivered. The rest didn't.

---

[CH11 | 12:55-14:03 | worldview_upgrade]

Step back.

The economics here are paradoxical.

Lottery tickets are the most predictable revenue stream in retail. The state sets the price, controls the inventory, guarantees the payout structure, and wires your commission like clockwork.

Compare that to a restaurant, where you're guessing at demand every night. Or a clothing store, where you're betting on trends six months out.

With lottery, the product is standardized, the margin is fixed, and the customer base is habit-driven. It's as close to a sure thing as retail gets.

But — and this is the whole game — that sure thing only pays if people walk through your door.

And whether they walk through your door depends on variables the lottery commission doesn't control: your lease terms, your location visibility, your parking, your neighborhood income distribution, your ability to float working capital through a rough quarter.

The guaranteed revenue stream is betting on everything *around* it not failing.

The floor is unbreakable. What you build on top of it isn't.

---

[CH12 | 14:03-16:00 | closure]

So what does success actually look like?

Small-scale scenario: convenience store, lottery as add-on revenue. Initial investment $10,000 to $15,000 for equipment and first inventory. Monthly lottery sales: $40,000. Commission: $2,400. After terminal lease and minor labor allocation, net monthly contribution: $1,800 to $2,000. Add ancillary sales from foot traffic, and you're clearing $25,000 to $30,000 annually from the lottery line alone. Payback in under a year.

Large-scale scenario: dedicated multi-location operator. Three storefronts, $400,000 total investment. Combined annual lottery sales: $6 million. Commission: $360,000 to $420,000. After rent, labor, and overhead, net profit margin sits around 8% to 12% — call it $35,000 to $50,000 per location.

But here's the inversion.

At that scale, lottery commission is no longer the main profit driver. It's the traffic driver.

Ancillary sales — cigarettes, beverages, snacks, phone cards, money orders — now account for 50% to 60% of gross profit. The lottery business became the customer acquisition engine for a convenience retail operation.

Real example: a regional chain in Texas started with lottery, now runs 12 locations. Lottery still does $15 million annually across all stores, but tobacco and beverage margins deliver more profit per square foot.

The business stopped being a lottery store and became a high-traffic retail location that uses lottery as the hook.

That's the endgame for anyone who survives long enough to scale.

The math guarantees the revenue. Your job is to guarantee everything the math doesn't cover.

Optimized Script

[CH01 | 00:00-00:42 | promise_setup]

So you want to own a lottery store.

Makes sense. It's the only business where probability guarantees profit on every ticket sold — and half the people who open one still go broke within three years.

Here's the problem: selling lottery tickets is mathematically bulletproof revenue. The state pays you a commission on everything that moves through your register. Every scratch-off, every Powerball, every draw game.

And yet lottery retailers close constantly.

So what breaks? Stick with me, and by the end you'll understand exactly how a guaranteed revenue stream still puts owners out of business — and what separates the ones who survive.

---

[CH02 | 00:42-01:34 | context_expansion]

Let's start with what it costs to get in.

Three tiers.

Bottom tier: you rent a corner inside an existing convenience store. Lottery machine, display rack, maybe eight square feet. You're looking at $5,000 to $15,000 in equipment and first inventory. Think gas stations and delis.

Middle tier: a standalone storefront. Now you're signing a lease, installing security, building out shelving, stocking a full wall of instant tickets. $50,000 to $120,000 all-in.

Top tier: franchise or multi-location operation. You're not just selling tickets, you're building a regional brand. Initial investment starts at $250,000 and can run past half a million.

The gap between tiers isn't just money. It's scale, margin compression, and infrastructure weight.

---

[CH03 | 01:34-02:49 | evidence_build]

But the real entry ticket isn't cash.

It's permission.

Most states cap the total number of lottery licenses. In tight markets, zero new licenses get issued for years. Want in? You buy out someone who already has one, or you wait until someone closes.

Then there's geography. Some states require population density thresholds — you can't open within a certain radius of an existing retailer unless the area supports it. Minimum distance between locations: 1,000 feet, half a mile, depends on the market.

And then the approval process itself. Background checks, credit reviews, site inspections. Timeline? Anywhere from 90 days to over a year. One applicant waited more than a year for final approval — by the time the license arrived, the lease had expired.

In tight markets, licenses trade like assets. A license with lottery rights can sell well above the underlying business value, just for the privilege of selling tickets.

The scarcity isn't accidental. It's engineered.

---

[CH04 | 02:49-04:52 | reveal]

Now the money.

Imagine you sell $100 worth of lottery tickets in a single transaction. Depending on the state and the game type, you keep between $5 and $7 of that.

That's your commission. Instant tickets — scratch-offs — typically pay 5% to 6%. Draw games like Powerball or Mega Millions pay a bit more, around 6% to 7%, because the state wants to incentivize promotion of big jackpot games.

So if your store moves $10,000 in lottery sales in a week, you're taking home $500 to $700 in commission.

Scale that up. A mid-volume standalone location doing $500,000 in annual lottery sales pulls roughly $30,000 in commission. A high-traffic convenience store pushing $2 million a year? $120,000 to $140,000.

But here's the split that matters: instant tickets vs draw games.

Instant tickets are impulse buys. Customer walks in, sees the wall, grabs three $5 scratch-offs on the way out. High frequency, low friction. Draw games require a slip, a selection, often a wait. Lower frequency, but bigger ticket averages when jackpots climb.

In practice, instant tickets account for 60% to 70% of total sales at most retailers. They're the engine. Draw games are the headline, but scratch-offs are the daily grind that keeps the register moving.

The state takes its cut first — roughly 60% to 65% goes to the prize pool, another 25% to 30% funds state programs. What's left after prizes and state allocation is split between administrative overhead and retailer commission.

Your slice is thin. But it's guaranteed.

---

[CH05 | 04:52-05:45 | reveal]

Here's the category nobody talks about: $1 and $2 instant tickets.

Lowest price point. Highest volume. Fastest repeat purchase cycle.

Commission rate on these? Often better than expensive tickets. Why? Because the state wants movement. A $1 ticket at 6% commission moves ten times faster than a $20 ticket at 5%. The math favors velocity.

And the customer? The one buying $2 scratch-offs every other day isn't the guy dropping $50 on a single $20 ticket. It's the regular. The construction worker stopping in every morning. The retiree buying two tickets with coffee.

That person — unremarkable, predictable, forgettable — is statistically your most valuable customer.

The $20 ticket buyer shows up when the jackpot hits $500 million. The $2 ticket buyer shows up 200 times a year.

Frequency beats ticket size. Always.

---

[CH06 | 05:45-06:31 | evidence_build]

So how do you engineer frequency?

Space.

The scratch-off wall goes behind the counter, eye level, fully stocked. Front and center, within arm's reach of the transaction.

The register? Positioned so the customer faces the wall while you ring them up. Thirty seconds of exposure. Enough time to scan, spot a new game, impulse-buy.

Successful retailers rotate stock weekly. New games get prime placement. Sold-out games disappear immediately — empty slots kill momentum.

And the counter itself: narrow the path, slow the exit. Not enough to frustrate, just enough to create a pause. That pause is where the add-on happens.

The goal isn't to sell once. It's to train the weekly return.

---

[CH07 | 06:31-07:18 | evidence_build]

Then there's loyalty.

Some states allow second-chance drawings. A customer loses on a scratch-off, enters the code online, gets another shot. It costs the retailer nothing, but it keeps the player engaged with your location.

Others permit in-store promotions: "Buy five tickets, get one free." The retailer eats the cost of that sixth ticket, but the math works if it converts a monthly buyer into a weekly buyer.

Look at lifetime value. An occasional customer spends maybe $200 a year. A regular? $1,500 to $2,000. The free ticket is a $5 investment to capture a $1,300 gap.

Casinos figured this out decades ago: give away the cheap thing to lock in the expensive behavior.

Lottery retailers are learning.

---

[CH08 | 07:18-08:35 | reveal]

Now the top of the pyramid.

The top 5% of lottery customers — high-frequency players spending $100 to $200 a week — can account for 30% to 40% of a store's total commission revenue.

One case: a retailer reported a single customer who spent $15,000 in a year on scratch-offs. At 6% commission, that's $900 from one person. Multiply by five or ten regulars at that tier, and you've just covered rent.

But they don't only buy lottery tickets.

They buy cigarettes. Energy drinks. Snacks. Lottery traffic is foot traffic, and foot traffic converts.

Gross margin on tobacco: 8% to 12%. On beverages: 20% to 35%. On packaged snacks: 25% to 40%. A high-volume lottery store in a good location can pull an additional $40,000 to $80,000 annually from ancillary sales driven by lottery customers.

The formula is:

**Commission rate × sales volume × purchase frequency × ancillary conversion**

Optimize any one variable, revenue climbs. Optimize all four, you're running a real business.

This is how a lottery store works when it works.

---

[CH09 | 08:35-10:46 | conflict_escalation]

Now the part that kills people.

Rent. For a standalone storefront in a decent location, you're paying $2,500 to $6,000 a month. High-traffic urban zones? Double that.

Labor. You can't leave a lottery terminal unattended. Minimum one employee per shift, often two. At $15/hour, that's $30,000 to $50,000 annually for basic coverage.

The lottery terminal itself: leased from the state lottery commission, usually $50 to $150 per month depending on the state. Non-negotiable.

Inventory. Instant tickets require upfront cash. You order $10,000 in scratch-offs, you pay $10,000. If they don't sell, you're holding dead inventory. The state eventually takes them back, but you've tied up cash for weeks or months.

Then there's the state's cut on your total revenue — not just prizes. Some states charge a licensing fee, an annual renewal, or a percentage override on gross sales. It's small, 1% to 2%, but it's another line item.

And cash handling. Lottery retailers move a lot of cash. Armored car pickup, safe rental, theft insurance, cash variance — it adds up. Estimate $500 to $1,500 a month depending on volume.

Oh, and unredeemed ticket liability. If you sell a winning ticket and the customer never claims it, the state keeps the prize, but you still owe them the funds for the ticket sold. It's rare, but it's a hidden float cost.

Add it up. Let's say you're pulling $40,000 in annual lottery commission. Rent takes $36,000. Labor takes $40,000. You're already underwater before utilities, insurance, inventory float, and terminal lease.

The commission is guaranteed. Everything else is a knife fight.

---

[CH10 | 10:46-12:55 | conflict_escalation]

Real failure looks like this.

Case one: a suburban strip mall. Investor opens a standalone lottery shop. Total buildout: $90,000. Projected annual sales: $1.2 million based on nearby demographics.

Actual sales: $320,000. Turns out the demographics were right, but the foot traffic was wrong. The anchor tenant — a grocery store — had closed six months earlier. No anchor, no traffic. Store lasted 11 months, closed owing $30,000 in back rent, sold fixtures for $8,000 — pennies on the dollar against the $90,000 buildout.

Lesson: foot traffic isn't a demographic projection. It's a physical headcount you verify in person, at the hours your customers actually shop.

Case two: an experienced retailer opens a second location with $50,000 in startup capital. Rent is $4,000/month, labor is $3,500/month, fixed costs run $8,000 monthly before inventory.

Sales start slower than expected. He dips into working capital to cover month two. Then month three. By month five, he's tapped out. Lottery sales were fine — $25,000 in commission over five months — but it wasn't enough to cover the burn rate. Closed after six months, lost the entire $50,000, and still owed on the terminal lease and remaining inventory float.

Lesson: don't open on a cash cushion that assumes perfection from day one. Budget for a slow ramp, or don't open at all.

Both cases share the same pattern: the revenue model worked. The math was sound. Location or cash flow broke them.

The commission delivered. The rest didn't.

---

[CH11 | 12:55-14:03 | worldview_upgrade]

Step back.

The economics here are paradoxical.

Lottery tickets are the most predictable revenue stream in retail. The state sets the price, controls the inventory, guarantees the payout structure, and wires your commission like clockwork.

Compare that to a restaurant, where you're guessing at demand every night. Or a clothing store, where you're betting on trends six months out.

With lottery, the product is standardized, the margin is fixed, and the customer base is habit-driven. It's as close to a sure thing as retail gets.

But — and this is the whole game — that sure thing only pays if people walk through your door.

And whether they walk through your door depends on variables the lottery commission doesn't control: your lease terms, your location visibility, your parking, your neighborhood income distribution, your ability to float working capital through a rough quarter.

The guaranteed revenue stream is betting on everything *around* it not failing.

The floor is unbreakable. Whatever you raise on top of it can still come down.

---

[CH12 | 14:03-16:00 | closure]

So what does success actually look like?

Small-scale scenario: convenience store, lottery as add-on revenue. Initial investment $10,000 to $15,000 for equipment and first inventory. Monthly lottery sales: $40,000. Commission: $2,400. After terminal lease and minor labor allocation, net monthly contribution: $1,800 to $2,000. Add ancillary sales from foot traffic, and you're clearing $25,000 to $30,000 annually from the lottery line alone. Payback in under a year.

Large-scale scenario: dedicated multi-location operator. Three storefronts, $400,000 total investment. Combined annual lottery sales: $6 million. Commission: $360,000 to $420,000. After rent, labor, and overhead, net profit margin sits around 8% to 12% — call it $35,000 to $50,000 per location.

But here's the inversion.

At that scale, lottery commission is no longer the main profit driver. It's the traffic driver.

Ancillary sales — cigarettes, beverages, snacks, phone cards, money orders — now account for 50% to 60% of gross profit. The lottery business became the customer acquisition engine for a convenience retail operation.

Think of a regional chain that started with lottery and grew to a dozen locations. Lottery still moves millions annually across all stores, but tobacco and beverage margins deliver more profit per square foot.

The business stopped being a lottery store and became a high-traffic retail location that uses lottery as the hook.

That's the endgame for anyone who survives long enough to scale.

The math guarantees the revenue. Your job is to guarantee everything the math doesn't cover.

But the real entry ticket isn't cash.

It's permission.

Most states cap the total number of lottery licenses. In tight markets, zero new licenses get issued for years. Want in? You buy out someone who already has one, or you wait until someone closes.

Then there's geography. Some states require population density thresholds — you can't open within a certain radius of an existing retailer unless the area supports it. Minimum distance between locations: 1,000 feet, half a mile, depends on the market.

And then the approval process itself. Background checks, credit reviews, site inspections. Timeline? Anywhere from 90 days to over a year. One applicant waited more than a year for final approval — by the time the license arrived, the lease had expired.

The scarcity isn't accidental. It's engineered.

[CH04 | 02:49-04:52 | reveal]

Now the money.

Imagine you sell $100 worth of lottery tickets in a single transaction. Depending on the state and the game type, you keep between $5 and $7 of that.

That's your commission. Instant tickets — scratch-offs — typically pay 5% to 6%. Draw games like Powerball or Mega Millions pay a bit more, around 6% to 7%, because the state wants to incentivize promotion of big jackpot games.

So if your store moves $10,000 in lottery sales in a week, you're taking home $500 to $700 in commission.

Scale that up. A mid-volume standalone location doing $500,000 in annual lottery sales pulls roughly $30,000 in commission. A high-traffic convenience store pushing $2 million a year? $120,000 to $140,000.

But here's the split that matters: instant tickets vs draw games.

Instant tickets are impulse buys. Customer walks in, sees the wall, grabs three $5 scratch-offs on the way out. High frequency, low friction. Draw games require a slip, a selection, often a wait. Lower frequency, but bigger ticket averages when jackpots climb.

In practice, instant tickets account for 60% to 70% of total sales at most retailers. They're the engine. Draw games are the headline, but scratch-offs are the daily grind that keeps the register moving.

The state takes its cut first — roughly 60% to 65% goes to the prize pool, another 25% to 30% funds state programs. What's left after prizes and state allocation is split between administrative overhead and retailer commission.

Your slice is thin. But it's guaranteed.

[CH05 | 04:52-05:45 | reveal]

Here's the category nobody talks about: $1 and $2 instant tickets.

Lowest price point. Highest volume. Fastest repeat purchase cycle.

Commission rate on these? Often better than expensive tickets. Why? Because the state wants movement. A $1 ticket at 6% commission moves ten times faster than a $20 ticket at 5%. The math favors velocity.

And the customer? The one buying $2 scratch-offs every other day isn't the guy dropping $50 on a single $20 ticket. It's the regular. The construction worker stopping in every morning. The retiree buying two tickets with coffee.

That person — unremarkable, predictable, forgettable — is statistically your most valuable customer.

The $20 ticket buyer shows up when the jackpot hits $500 million. The $2 ticket buyer shows up 200 times a year.

Frequency beats ticket size. Always.

So how do you engineer frequency?

Space.

The scratch-off wall goes behind the counter, eye level, fully stocked. Front and center, within arm's reach of the transaction.

The register? Positioned so the customer faces the wall while you ring them up. Thirty seconds of exposure. Enough time to scan, spot a new game, impulse-buy.

Successful retailers rotate stock weekly. New games get prime placement. Sold-out games disappear immediately — empty slots kill momentum.

And the counter itself: narrow the path, slow the exit. Not enough to frustrate, just enough to create a pause. That pause is where the add-on happens.

The goal isn't to sell once. It's to train the weekly return.

Then there's loyalty.

Some states allow second-chance drawings. A customer loses on a scratch-off, enters the code online, gets another shot. It costs the retailer nothing, but it keeps the player engaged with your location.

Others permit in-store promotions: "Buy five tickets, get one free." The retailer eats the cost of that sixth ticket, but the math works if it converts a monthly buyer into a weekly buyer.

Look at lifetime value. An occasional customer spends maybe $200 a year. A regular? $1,500 to $2,000. The free ticket is a $5 investment to capture a $1,300 gap.

Casinos figured this out decades ago: give away the cheap thing to lock in the expensive behavior.

Lottery retailers are learning.

Now the top of the pyramid.

The top 5% of lottery customers — high-frequency players spending $100 to $200 a week — can account for 30% to 40% of a store's total commission revenue.

One case: a retailer reported a single customer who spent $15,000 in a year on scratch-offs. At 6% commission, that's $900 from one person. Multiply by five or ten regulars at that tier, and you've just covered rent.

But they don't only buy lottery tickets.

They buy cigarettes. Energy drinks. Snacks. Lottery traffic is foot traffic, and foot traffic converts.

Gross margin on tobacco: 8% to 12%. On beverages: 20% to 35%. On packaged snacks: 25% to 40%. A high-volume lottery store in a good location can pull an additional $40,000 to $80,000 annually from ancillary sales driven by lottery customers.

The formula is:

**Commission rate × sales volume × purchase frequency × ancillary conversion**

Optimize any one variable, revenue climbs. Optimize all four, you're running a real business.

This is how a lottery store works when it works.

Now the part that kills people.

Rent. For a standalone storefront in a decent location, you're paying $2,500 to $6,000 a month. High-traffic urban zones? Double that.

Labor. You can't leave a lottery terminal unattended. Minimum one employee per shift, often two. At $15/hour, that's $30,000 to $50,000 annually for basic coverage.

The lottery terminal itself: leased from the state lottery commission, usually $50 to $150 per month depending on the state. Non-negotiable.

Inventory. Instant tickets require upfront cash. You order $10,000 in scratch-offs, you pay $10,000. If they don't sell, you're holding dead inventory. The state eventually takes them back, but you've tied up cash for weeks or months.

Then there's the state's cut on your total revenue — not just prizes. Some states charge a licensing fee, an annual renewal, or a percentage override on gross sales. It's small, 1% to 2%, but it's another line item.

And cash handling. Lottery retailers move a lot of cash. Armored car pickup, safe rental, theft insurance, cash variance — it adds up. Estimate $500 to $1,500 a month depending on volume.

Oh, and unredeemed ticket liability. If you sell a winning ticket and the customer never claims it, the state keeps the prize, but you still owe them the funds for the ticket sold. It's rare, but it's a hidden float cost.

Add it up. Let's say you're pulling $40,000 in annual lottery commission. Rent takes $36,000. Labor takes $40,000. You're already underwater before utilities, insurance, inventory float, and terminal lease.

The commission is guaranteed. Everything else is a knife fight.

Real failure looks like this.

Case two: an experienced retailer opens a second location with $50,000 in startup capital. Rent is $4,000/month, labor is $3,500/month, fixed costs run $8,000 monthly before inventory.

Sales start slower than expected. He dips into working capital to cover month two. Then month three. By month five, he's tapped out. Lottery sales were fine — $25,000 in commission over five months — but it wasn't enough to cover the burn rate. Closed after six months, lost the entire $50,000, and still owed on the terminal lease and remaining inventory float.

Lesson: don't open on a cash cushion that assumes perfection from day one. Budget for a slow ramp, or don't open at all.

The commission delivered. The rest didn't.

Step back.

The economics here are paradoxical.

Lottery tickets are the most predictable revenue stream in retail. The state sets the price, controls the inventory, guarantees the payout structure, and wires your commission like clockwork.

Compare that to a restaurant, where you're guessing at demand every night. Or a clothing store, where you're betting on trends six months out.

With lottery, the product is standardized, the margin is fixed, and the customer base is habit-driven. It's as close to a sure thing as retail gets.

But — and this is the whole game — that sure thing only pays if people walk through your door.

And whether they walk through your door depends on variables the lottery commission doesn't control: your lease terms, your location visibility, your parking, your neighborhood income distribution, your ability to float working capital through a rough quarter.

The guaranteed revenue stream is betting on everything *around* it not failing.

The floor is unbreakable. Whatever you raise on top of it can still come down.

At that scale, lottery commission is no longer the main profit driver. It's the traffic driver.

That's the endgame for anyone who survives long enough to scale.

The math guarantees the revenue. Your job is to guarantee everything the math doesn't cover.
